title: Wireless Security: the air as perimeter
description: From WEP to WPA3: the 4-way handshake, classic attacks (deauth, evil twin) and how a WiFi network is properly audited.

1.title: WEP, WPA2 and the 4-way handshake
1.body:
## The evolutionary line

| Generation | Year | Key | Broken by |
|---|---|---|---|
| WEP | 1999 | RC4, 24-bit IV | Statistics (minutes) |
| WPA-TKIP | 2003 | patch on top of WEP | TKIP (deprecated) |
| WPA2-CCMP | 2004 | AES + 4-way handshake | Offline cracking of a weak PSK |
| WPA3-SAE | 2018 | password-authenticated | Downgrade/implementation bugs |

## The 4-way handshake (the heart of WPA2)

Four messages between the client and the AP that prove both know the
PSK **without revealing it** and derive the session keys. The attacker only
needs to CAPTURE it:

```bash
# Audit of YOUR network (aircrack-ng suite):
sudo airmon-ng start wlan0                  # monitor mode
sudo airodump-ng wlan0mon                   # see networks and clients
sudo airodump-ng -c 6 --bssid AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF -w captura wlan0mon
# (wait for a client to connect — or force it: task 2)

# Offline crack of the captured handshake:
aircrack-ng -w /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt captura-01.cap
# hashcat equivalent: -m 22000 (hcxpaxke/hccapx format)
```

The brute force is offline (GPU speed) but the derivation is
EXPENSIVE (PBKDF2 4096×): a PSK of 12+ random characters holds out for
decades. "MiFibra-2024" falls within the hour.

## The SSID detail

The PSK is hashed with the SSID as its salt — that's why default SSIDs
("MOVISTAR_XXXX") have massive precomputed tables (36k SSIDs ×
rockyou). Changing the default SSID breaks those tables. It's the most
underrated technical reason behind "rename your WiFi".

## WPA3: SAE

SAE replaces the handshake with a Dragonfly-style exchange where every
attempt requires interacting with the AP: there's nothing to crack
offline. The practical weaknesses today: downgrades to WPA2
(misconfigured transition mode), implementation bugs (Dragonblood)
and... the user connecting to the evil twin without the cryptography
mattering at all — the next task.

seguridad-wireless-t01-q01.prompt: What is the design weakness that makes WEP break in minutes?
seguridad-wireless-t01-q01.hint: Look at the WEP row in the table: which cipher it uses and how big its initialization vector (IV) is. What happens when such a small IV repeats?

options.a: It uses AES with 64-bit keys, too short to resist GPU brute force
options.b: It sends the password in cleartext inside every access point's beacon
options.c: It uses RC4 with 24-bit IVs that repeat and leak the key after few captured packets
options.d: It relies on an 8-digit WPS PIN that can be brute-forced

seguridad-wireless-t01-q02.prompt: Which exchange establishes the session key in WPA2-Personal and is THE capture target in an audit?
seguridad-wireless-t01-q02.hint: The 4-way handshake (WPA handshake): the keys are derived from it, and the PSK is cracked offline against it

seguridad-wireless-t01-q03.prompt: In WPA-Personal, which two pieces of data are combined (PBKDF2, 4096 iterations) to derive the key that hashcat/aircrack test when cracking the password offline?
seguridad-wireless-t01-q03.hint: Review "The SSID detail": one of the two pieces acts as a salt, which is why default network names have precomputed tables.

options.a: The SSID (as salt) and the password (PSK)
options.b: The AP's MAC address and the channel number
options.c: The 24-bit IV and the RC4 key
options.d: The RADIUS server certificate and its private key

seguridad-wireless-t01-q04.prompt: Which WPA3 mechanism eliminated offline handshake cracking, and what practical weakness remains when the configuration is weak?
seguridad-wireless-t01-q04.hint: Look at the last row of the table and the "WPA3" section: a Dragonfly-style exchange… and what happens with a misconfigured transition mode.

options.c: EAP-TLS; the lack of an in-house PKI
options.d: SAE (Dragonfly); downgrades to WPA2 (transition mode) and bugs such as Dragonblood

2.title: Deauth and evil twin: attacking trust
2.body:
## Deauth: the shove

Classic 802.11 doesn't authenticate management frames: anyone can
inject a "disconnect" signed as if it came from the AP:

```bash
# Against YOUR lab network:
sudo aireplay-ng -0 3 -a AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF -c CLIENTMAC wlan0mon
#   -0 3: 3 deauth packets
#   The client reconnects → a fresh handshake in your capture
```

With WPA3 management frames are protected (SAE/PMF) and the classic deauth
dies. With WPA2 it still works on every network without
`ieee80211w=1` (protected management frames) — which is almost all of them.

## Evil twin: the copy

```
[Victim] ──connects──▶ [Attacker AP "MiFibra-A1B2"] ──internet──▶ [MITM attacker]
                              same ESSID, channel with a better signal or after a mass deauth
```

The modern kit (wifiphisher, hostapd + dnsmasq):

```bash
# hostapd with the cloned ESSID + dnsmasq serving fake DHCP/DNS
# → phishing of the portal (router, Google, office) → credentials
# → or HTTPS stripping + installation (the hard way, detected by the browser)
```

Correct cryptography (HTTPS with HSTS) survives the MITM; a
user asked to log in on a fake portal doesn't. That's why the evil twin is
the phishing of the air: the fight is about UX and training, not ciphers.

## Legitimate wireless auditing — the complete kit

| Phase | Tool |
|---|---|
| Monitor mode + discovery | airmon-ng, airodump-ng, kismet |
| Handshake capture | airodump-ng (+ a targeted deauth) |
| Offline crack | aircrack-ng / hashcat -m 22000 |
| Rogue detection | kismet (twin AP alerts), Wireshark |
| WPS (the other hole) | reaver (WPS PIN brute force — networks with WPS enabled) |

**The legal framework**: in almost every jurisdiction, intercepting other people's
networks (even "just capturing") is a crime. These techniques are
practiced on YOUR lab network (an old AP + two WiFi cards
that support monitor mode — the classic Alfa AWUS036ACH) or on
platforms with dedicated environments.

seguridad-wireless-t02-q01.prompt: What does a deauthentication attack do, and which 802.11 weakness does it exploit?
seguridad-wireless-t02-q01.hint: Review "Deauth: the shove": are management frames authenticated in classic 802.11? And what does the attacker gain every time the client reconnects?

options.a: It floods the channel with radio noise until the AP reboots and forgets its PSK
options.b: It forges disconnection frames (unauthenticated in 802.11) and forces reconnections with fresh handshakes
options.c: It clones the legitimate AP's ESSID so that clients connect to the attacker
options.d: It decrypts data frames using the router's default password

seguridad-wireless-t02-q02.hint: Look at the diagram in "Evil twin: the copy": which network name does the attacker's AP advertise, and why does the client connect to it?

options.a: A fake AP advertising the same ESSID as the legitimate one so that clients connect to it
options.b: A legitimate repeater that extends the network's coverage
options.c: Malware that clones the victim's WiFi card
options.d: A second handshake capture to crack it twice as fast

seguridad-wireless-t02-q03.prompt: In WPA-Enterprise (802.1X), which mechanism would have prevented the evil twin's credential capture, and what does deploying it require?
seguridad-wireless-t02-q03.hint: The fake AP can't present the legitimate server's cryptographic identity… as long as the client checks it and the user doesn't click 'accept' on the warning.

options.a: Hiding the SSID; it requires nothing else
options.b: MAC address filtering; it requires maintaining a client allowlist
options.c: Validating the server certificate (EAP-TLS); it requires your own PKI
options.d: Enabling WPS; it requires an 8-digit PIN per device

seguridad-wireless-t02-q04.prompt: Why are open networks with a captive portal the evil twin's natural habitat?
seguridad-wireless-t02-q04.hint: Think about user habits, not cryptography: over the air "the fight is about UX and training".

options.a: Because they use WPA3 and SAE doesn't protect login pages
options.b: Because captive portals share the PSK with every client
options.c: Because the legitimate AP of an open network doesn't send beacons
options.d: Because users are used to accepting login portals and odd certificates, so they don't get suspicious
